INTRODUCTION 
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is currently working on the 
Artemis Project, sending astronauts to the moon for the first time in decades, with the hopes of 
establishing a permanent settlement on the moon. Beyond this, other ventures have their sights set 
forward towards Mars, with the hopes of establishing a permanent settlement on the planet. With 
space travel and colonization, factors such as food growth must be investigated. 
A group of 10 undergraduate students at Southwestern Oklahoma State University recently 
competed in the Plant Mars Challenge, hosted by the Institute of Competition Sciences. This team 
was funded by the Oklahoma Space Grant Consortium. The primary goal was to sustain crop 
growth in simulated Mars regolith. The international challenge was to have the highest plant yield 
in a 8-week growth period using simulated Mars-regolith, which is chemically similar to the 
composition of substrate on Mars. This regolith was produced by the University of Central 
Florida’s CLASS Exolith Laboratory, and supplied by the competition. As part of this competition, 
at least 50% of the total volume of the pot must be filled with Mars-regolith or Earth soil. Beyond 
this requirement, all of our pots contained the following additives: activated charcoal, coconut coir, 
Epsom salt, and perlite. 
As there were water logging issues during our participation in the previous year’s 
competition, we included additives that are beneficial in the prevention of water logging. Coconut 
coir, activated charcoal, and perlite all served to do this by aerating the soil (Activated Charcoal, 
n.d.; Sears, 2001; Tuckeldoe et al., 2023). In addition to this benefit, perlite also served as a source 
of the beneficial nutrient potassium (Sears, 2001). For the last of the universal soil components, 
we used Epsom salt. Epsom salt was used as it is a provider of magnesium which promotes high 
levels of chlorophyll production (Epsom, 2021). For our experimental regolith additives, we

Page 3 of 16 
wanted to look at how using mammalian fecal matter compared to using worm castings. We also 
wanted to measure differences between microbes by observing differences in pots with bacteria 
added and pots with mycorrhizae added. We observed how our chosen dependent variables – mass 
of plant, chlorophyll leaf content, seed germination, plant color, and plant height – differed within 
the different additives. 
Our team chose two commercial microbial soil additives. Mikro-H2O© rhizobacteria was 
chosen as it has been shown to significantly aid in increasing germination and growth rates 
(Gholami, 2009). This bacteria increases the length of the radicle, the part of the plant embryo 
that later becomes the plant’s primary root, which increases its surface area and water uptake 
(Pérez, 2023). While also promoting plant growth, Rhizobium leguminosarum was chosen 
because it differs from our other microbial additive because it is a nitrogen-fixing bacteria 
(Yanni, 2010). Nitrogen-fixing bacteria take nitrogen from the environment and convert it most 
commonly into ammonia for plants to take in at their roots, as they cannot convert it themselves 
(Cocking, 2000). Unknown microbes were also present within the unsterilized rabbit droppings 
and the vermicompost tea. 
Would these additions to our soil allow our Mars soil to become more fertile and yield 
better results for our crops? The interactions between plants and bacteria have been known to be 
beneficial to plant growth. (Palacio et al., 2023). Gut bacteria from mammals have been known to 
be beneficial for plant growth. Additionally, rabbit compost specifically could lead to increased 
fruit weight (Adi et al., 2020). This partially inspired our idea of rabbit tea. Vermicompost is 
known to have many beneficial effects on plants, like growth, yield, and quality, and also has been 
shown to increase germination (Vuković et al., 2021). In addition to this, by introducing rhizobia 
bacteria into our soil, the nitrogen fixation in our legumes could lead to a higher yield and overall

Page 4 of 16 
more growth due to the relationship formed with the bacteria (Laysa et al., 2022). These factors 
combined with the plant choices that were made to have faster growing plants could lead to higher 
yield and faster growth. 
Each pot contained four crops: peas, basil, spinach, and lettuce. The species are Lizard 
Spinach (Spinacia oleracea), Red Rubin Basil (Ocimum basilicum), Patio Pride Snap Peas (Pisum 
sativum), and Rhone Lettuce (Lactuca sativa). Four plants were grown in each pot to continue our 
observations of diversity between crops. This was to study biodiversity within crop selections. 
Basil was grown with the intent of boosting morale, because of its ability to add flavor to dishes. 
Rubin basil is slow to bolt, so there is a longer harvest time. We chose the Lizard Spinach because 
it can be harvested in about 1 month. This crop also has good regrowth once leaves are cut from 
harvest. This would be especially useful in real-life application because we would need crops that 
could keep yielding food consistently as opposed to crops that could only be harvested once. 
Spinach carries many different minerals and vitamins that are essential and beneficial to the human 
body like vitamin A, C, E, and K, as well as zinc, magnesium, and phosphorus (Lasya, 2022). It is 
also rich in lutein, calcium, and iron (Rueda et al., 2022). It is a versatile crop that can be prepared 
in several ways, which could keep the food choices less limited. 
Patio pride snap peas were chosen as a continuation of the previous SWOSU to Mars team 
experiments. They grow well in the containers and vertical growth allows for more food production 
in small spaces. The pods add a substantial amount of mass, and the leaves could also be consumed. 
Peas form a symbiotic relationship with root-nodulating diazotrophic bacteria, known as rhizobia. 
The roots of pea plants also form mycorrhizal associations with arbuscular fungi, or the fungal 
microbes that colonize the area surrounding the roots of plants (Kalapchieva et al., 2023).

Page 5 of 16 
We chose Rhone lettuce because it can be harvested in 52 days, which is within our 
timeframe. It also produces high yields. Head lettuce was avoided, and leaf lettuce was chosen 
because head lettuce takes longer to produce and can only be harvested once. Rhone is a dark leaf 
lettuce, which can be considered to have more nutrient content. Lettuce is generally considered 
low in nutritional value, but there have been studies that showed nutrient content varies on the 
lettuce type, and that darker colors such as red, purple, and black contain more nutrients as well. 
(Kim et al., 2016). 
We used microbes, rabbit tea, charcoal, and perlite to see if they were able to get food 
growth in the Mars regrowth plants, to be able to see in future plants what was able to help the 
plant growth and what didn’t help the plant growth. We hypothesized that unsterilized rabbit tea, 
vermicompost, fungi, and bacteria would result in differences in plant growth and the amount of 
chlorophyll present. 
 
The independent variables we measured throughout the course of this challenge are 
unsterilized rabbit tea, vermicompost (worm castings) tea, unsterilized rabbit droppings, rhizobia 
bacteria, and high fungal soil microbes. Germination of seeds, plant height, plant mass, and 
chlorophyll content of leaves (measured by color) are the dependent variables that were measured 
throughout the Plant Mars challenge. 
 
The variables that were controlled during our experiment were the amount of water the 
plants receive, pot placement (within a climate-controlled greenhouse on campus), and some of 
the soil additives. The soil additives that remained constant throughout our 16 pots were 
horticultural charcoal, Epsom salt, coconut coir, and perlite.

METHODS 
All of our seeds were ordered from Johnny Seeds, and they were not given any treatments 
prior to planting. Seeds were planted in the soil mixtures in 4 separate quadrants of the pots (Figure 
1). In each pot, two Patio Pride snap pea seeds, three Rhone lettuce seeds, four Red Rubin basil 
seeds, and three Lizard spinach seeds were planted. The seeds were then watered gently, but 
thoroughly, using a pipette. They were kept on a bottom watering schedule thereafter. The pots 
were soaked in dechlorinated water for at least 15 minutes 2-3 times per week throughout the 
growth period. 
 
Figure 1: Diagram of the pots of soil with the contents. On the left, 
the number of seeds are shown. On the right, the location of the 
plants are split into quadrants, with spinach in the top left (s), peas 
in the top right (p), basil in the bottom left (b), and lettuce in the 
bottom right (l). 
 
Potting and planting started on February 17th. Ten pots of mixed Mars regolith were used 
with different additives. The same additives were added to Earth controls. The soil in each pot 
consisted of (by volume): 250 milliliters (mL) of Mars regolith or Earth soil, 100 mL of coconut 
coir, a pinch of Epsom salt (0.7 grams), 75 mL of perlite, 50mL of either sterilized or unsterilized 
rabbit droppings, and 40 mL of activated charcoal. Since there was a smaller amount of Epsom

Page 7 of 16 
salt, that was mixed in each pot separately. Other soil additives were mixed in large batches and 
divided between the pots. There were 5 different variable soil additives applied to 5 sets of 2 pots. 
After 3 weeks, commercially available products Mikro-H2O©, which contains Bacillus 
amyloliquefaciens and Bacillus subtilis, and Exceed Superior Legume Inoculant, which contains 
Rhizobium leguminosarum bv. viceae, Bradyrhizobium spp., and Rhizobium leguminosarum bv. 
phaseoli, were mixed in water and added to their respective pots during watering. All pots

DISCUSSION 
 
To continue on last year’s project, we planted multiple crops in each pot. This was to assess 
whether crops grew well together, since monocultures inhibit biodiversity. Growing multiple 
species per pot would also be a way to maximize surface area. The team took spacecraft storage 
into consideration, selecting soil components that could easily be packed in small spaces. We also 
decided against using materials like potting soil in the regolith mix, since it was assumed that there 
would be a shortage or problem with Earth soil if Mars was being colonized. The greenhouse we 
used did not account for differences in gravitational pull. We did not use artificial lighting because 
of the similarities in light availability between Earth and Mars. 
 
An analysis on last year's soil was completed by Oklahoma State University’s Soil, Water, 
and Forage Analytical Laboratory (SWFAL). This analysis showed that Mars-regolith had an 
average pH of 7.6, compared to the average Oklahoma soil pH of 6.3. The focus of the soil mixture 
was to ensure the soil would not become too alkaline throughout the growing period. The 
phosphorus in the Mars-regolith averaged to 1 pound per square meter (lb/m2). Potassium results 
are 283 lbs/m2. The recommended potassium is 85 lbs/acre (1 acre is equivalent to 4,046.86 m2). 
The nitrate nitrogen (NO3-N) concentration in the Mars soil is 0.2 per square meter. The 
recommended concentration of NO3-N is 92.903 per square meter. 
Moving forward, the team might experiment with different crops or soil mixtures. The ratio 
of soil additives seemed to work well, but there may be a different combination that would allow 
for a larger biomass in the Mars pots. It would also be interesting to do part of the treatments with 
one crop vs. treatments with multiple crops.

Page 13 of 16 
CONCLUSIONS 
 
Unlike last season, we managed to have sustained growth in the Mars pots for the entire 8-
week growth period. We also did not experience many issues due to waterlogging, and the plants 
did not ever completely dry out. However, only spinach managed to grow in the Mars treatment, 
and it took about 3 weeks longer to germinate than the plants in Earth treatments. This might 
indicate that the Mars soil mixture contained inhibitory elements that severely stunted germination. 
The spinach in the Mars treatments had a hue that was more yellow than Earth spinach, which 
could indicate a nitrogen deficiency. This could be confirmed or rejected after chemical analysis 
of the soil. 
 
The automatic pH indicator supplied did not give accurate readings, so we used pH strips. 
We ran out of the pH strips about halfway through the growth period. 
It seemed odd to the team that the fungi additives were beneficial in the Earth treatment, 
showing the highest biomass, but did not facilitate growth in the Mars fungal treatment. While we 
did not get much growth in the Mars treatment, we did observe that the worm castings and bacteria 
had slightly more biomass. These treatments could be bioremedies for agriculturalists to consider 
using as opposed to commercial fertilizers and pesticides. On Earth, a mycorrhizal treatment along 
with soil additives may increase yield. 
All of the Earth pots had growth, so the soil additives did not seem to inhibit crop 
production. The ratios used could provide a starting point for home gardeners or for crop 
production within greenhouses, where the soil could be mixed and the conditions match those used 
in our research.
